Seal vibrissae from harbor seals, elephant seals, and California sea lions were obtained and analyzed using 3D scanning, microscopy, and CT scans.
The pitch (P) and amplitude (a) of the undulations on the seal blades were varied, with some designs matching the specific P/a ratio and P/leading edge radius of the actual seal vibrissae.
CFD simulations were conducted at a Reynolds number of 100,000 based on inlet conditions and blade axial chord.
For the Sin1R0P5 seal blade, the average total pressure loss coefficient was reduced by around 50% to 0.069 compared to the baseline untreated blade.
The seal blades showed consistent performance improvements over the baseline configuration at incidence angles ranging from -37 to +10 degrees.
At the negative incidence angle of -37 degrees, the seal blade prevented separation on the pressure side that was observed for the untreated blade.
Hotwire surveys in the wake of the Sin1R0P5 seal blade showed a reduction in broadband frequency content and turbulence intensity compared to the untreated blade.
The researchers estimated that a fuel burn reduction of approximately 5% could be achieved for a fixed-wing aircraft by using the seal blade design.
The large thickness-to-chord ratio of the baseline turbine blade provided enough volume for potential internal flow control activities.
The researchers conducted a comprehensive literature review on biomimetic aerodynamic and acoustic applications, covering features from owls, whales, sharks, dragonflies, and more.
The researchers noted that the undulation amplitude could potentially be reduced towards the trailing edge, or undulation sweep could be introduced, to further optimize the blade design.
The experimental setup included the NASA SW-2 cascade wind tunnel facility, which was modified to accommodate testing of biomimetic and flow control test articles.
The CFD simulations used the NASA in-house Unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes code, Glenn-HT, with the SST - transition enabled two-equation model.
The researchers validated the CFD model against previous experimental data for the baseline turbine blade geometry.
The researchers observed that a smaller undulation pitch had a larger benefit on performance, while the amplitude of the undulation did not have a significant effect.
